lessons.title: Lab: Article 14 – is the classification reasonable?

story.title: The scheme for some, not all

scenes.text: A state announces a free-laptop scheme only for students of government colleges in rural districts. A student from an urban government college challenges it.
The state says rural students need more help. Is this valid classification?

steps.title: Equality before the law and equal protection
steps.body: Article 14 forbids arbitrary state action. The state may classify if there is an **intelligible differentia** distinguishing those grouped from others and the differentia has a **rational nexus** with the object of the law (State of West Bengal v Anwar Ali Sarkar and later cases). In E.P. Royappa (1974) the Supreme Court said arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body:
- Differentia: rural district colleges versus urban ones
- Object: reduce the digital divide
- Nexus: rural students have less access, so the nexus is plausible

The court would probably uphold it unless the classification is arbitrary or unevenly applied.

steps.title: Structure your answer
steps.body: State the rule, state the test, apply each limb, conclude.

items: Identify the classification made by the law
Ask whether there is an intelligible differentia
Ask whether the differentia has a rational nexus with the object
Conclude whether the law is valid

options: Equality before law and equal protection of laws

quiz.q: Arbitrariness is called the antithesis of equality in

lessons.title: Lab: Article 19 and the limits of free speech

scenes.text: A government orders a social media post criticising a minister to be removed under a law that punishes offensive messages.
The poster argues the law is too vague. In 2015 the Supreme Court dealt with a similar law.

steps.title: Freedoms and restrictions
steps.body:
Article 19(1)(a) protects speech and expression; 19(1)(b) to (g) protect assembly, association, movement, residence and profession. Reasonable restrictions are permitted only on the grounds listed in 19(2) to 19(6). For speech these include sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence.

In Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) the Court struck down section 66A of the IT Act as vague and over-broad, distinguishing discussion, advocacy and incitement.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: A restriction must fall within a listed ground. Embarrassing the government is not a ground.

lessons.title: Lab: Article 21 and the expanding right to life

scenes.text: A journalist's passport was impounded without giving reasons. She challenged it in the Supreme Court in 1978.
The question: can liberty be taken away by any procedure laid down by law, however unfair?

steps.title: From A.K. Gopalan to Maneka Gandhi
steps.body: Article 21: no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. In **Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978)** the Court held the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable, and Articles 14, 19 and 21 are linked. Since then Article 21 has covered the right to live with dignity, privacy, a clean environment, speedy trial, legal aid and more. **K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017)** held privacy to be a fundamental right. Article 21A gives free and compulsory education to children from 6 to 14.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Fundamental rights are enforceable by writ under Articles 32 and 226.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – writs and basic structure

story.title: The amendment that tried to oust the courts

scenes.text: Parliament passes a constitutional amendment saying no court may question certain laws. A citizen files a petition.
Which court, which article, and which writ?

steps.title: Writs and basic structure
steps.body:
Under Article 32 the Supreme Court and under Article 226 the High Courts issue writs: **habeas corpus** (produce the detained person), **mandamus** (command to perform a public duty), **certiorari** (quash a decision of a lower body), **prohibition** (stop proceedings) and **quo warranto** (by what authority an office is held).

In **Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973)** the Court held that Parliament's power under Article 368 does not allow it to alter the basic structure, which includes judicial review, supremacy of the Constitution and the rule of law. Minerva Mills (1980) reinforced this.

courses.title: Civil Procedure Code, 1908 – Basics
courses.summary: How a civil suit travels: jurisdiction, plaint, written statement, interim relief, res judicata, decree, appeal and execution, with practical drafting checks.
outcomes: Learners can determine which court has jurisdiction
Learners can list the contents of a plaint and written statement

lessons.title: Lab: Choose the court – subject, money and place

scenes.text: A Pune supplier is owed 8 lakh rupees by a Nagpur buyer under a contract signed in Mumbai and performed in Nagpur.
Where can the supplier file the suit?

steps.title: Three kinds of jurisdiction
steps.body:
- **Subject matter**: civil courts hear all suits of a civil nature unless barred (section 9)
- **Pecuniary**: the value of the suit decides which court tries it, fixed by state law
- **Territorial**: the suit is filed where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arises (section 20)

Immovable property suits are filed where the property lies (sections 16 to 18).

steps.title: Applying
steps.body: The buyer lives in Nagpur and the contract was performed there, so a Nagpur court has jurisdiction. The place of making (Mumbai) may also give a part of the cause of action.

lessons.title: Lab: Plaint and written statement checklist

scenes.text: A junior files a plaint without stating the cause of action or court fee. The registry returns it.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Pleadings
steps.body:
A suit starts with a **plaint** (Order VII): court name, plaintiff and defendant details, facts constituting the cause of action, jurisdiction, valuation and court fee, limitation, reliefs claimed and verification. The defendant files a **written statement** (Order VIII) within 30 days, extendable up to 90 days, admitting or denying each allegation specifically, with any set-off or counterclaim.

An Order VII Rule 11 application seeks rejection of a plaint, for example where no cause of action is disclosed or the suit is barred by law.

steps.title: Drafting rule
steps.body: Plead material facts, not evidence or law.

lessons.title: Lab: Res judicata, res sub judice and interim relief

story.title: Two suits on the same land

scenes.text: A man loses a title suit about his field and files a new suit on the same claim. Another person sues twice in two courts at once.
Meanwhile a neighbour starts cutting trees on the disputed plot.

steps.title: Barriers to repeat litigation
steps.body:
- **Res sub judice (section 10)**: a later suit on the same matter in issue between the same parties is stayed while the earlier suit is pending
- **Res judicata (section 11)**: a matter already finally decided between the same parties cannot be tried again

**Interim relief**: under Order XXXIX the court may grant a temporary injunction to preserve the position if the plaintiff shows a prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – decree, appeal and execution

story.title: Won the case, still no money

scenes.text: Meena gets a decree for 5 lakh rupees but the defendant does not pay.
What steps remain and what appeal rights exist?

steps.title: After judgment
steps.body: A **decree** formally expresses the court's decision. Remedies: first appeal on facts and law (section 96); second appeal only on a substantial question of law (section 100); review by the same court (section 114, Order XLVII); revision by the High Court (section 115). **Execution** is under Order XXI: attachment and sale of property, arrest and detention, garnishee orders or delivery of possession. Limitation Act, 1963 sets time limits for suits and appeals.

lessons.title: Lab: Frame issues from a moot proposition

scenes.text: Team Alpha receives a six-page moot proposition about data privacy, a startup, and a government notice.
They have two weeks. Where do they start?

steps.title: First reading
steps.body:
Read the proposition twice. First list facts by date. Then underline legal questions. Frame **issues** as questions that the court must decide, each tied to a statute or precedent. Order them logically, usually jurisdiction or maintainability first.

Typical structure: Statement of jurisdiction, statement of facts, issues, summary of arguments, arguments advanced, prayer.

steps.title: Neutral facts
steps.body: The facts in the memorial must be accurate and drawn from the proposition; advocacy belongs in the arguments.

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview – legal knowledge

story.title: Interview day at a law chambers

scenes.text: Karthik waits to meet a senior advocate who tests fundamentals before looking at marks.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: How to answer
steps.body: State the rule, give the case, apply to the facts and conclude. Be brief; admit gaps honestly.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Answer in your own words. The tool will compare your answer with key points and show a model answer afterwards.

rounds.q: What are the essentials of a valid contract under the Indian Contract Act?
rounds.model: Section 10 says agreements are contracts if made by free consent of competent parties for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and not expressly declared void. Writing and registration are needed only where a particular law requires them. I would test each element against the facts, for example capacity of a minor or coercion.
followups: What is the effect of a minor's agreement?

rounds.q: Explain the difference between strict liability and absolute liability.
rounds.model: Strict liability from Rylands v Fletcher applies to escape of a dangerous thing but allows exceptions such as act of God. In M.C. Mehta the Supreme Court evolved absolute liability for hazardous enterprises with no exceptions and compensation linked to the enterprise's capacity.
followups: Which case involved the oleum gas leak?

rounds.q: A police officer refuses to register an FIR for a cognizable offence. What can the complainant do under the BNSS?
points: send information to the superintendent of police
rounds.model: The complainant can send the information in writing to the Superintendent of Police, and if still not acted upon can approach a magistrate to direct investigation. The complainant may also use a zero FIR at any station or give information electronically. I would document the refusal and advise accordingly.

rounds.q: Which writ would you seek to challenge an order of a tribunal that exceeded its jurisdiction, and why?
rounds.model: Certiorari under Article 226 or 32 allows the High Court or Supreme Court to quash an order that is without jurisdiction or against natural justice. I would also check alternative remedies.

rounds.q: Why law, and what area do you want to practise in?
rounds.model: I chose law to help people resolve disputes fairly. I am drawn to civil litigation because I enjoy building arguments from documents. I want to learn under a senior, do careful research, and always follow professional ethics.
followups: Tell us about a moot or internship you learned from.

tips: Be honest about what you do not know

quiz.q: If you do not know a case, you should
options: Say so and reason from principle

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview – ethics and judgement

story.title: The client who wants to lie

scenes.text: A client asks you to submit a document you know is backdated.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Professional ethics
steps.body: Advocates owe duties to the court first, then to the client. They must not mislead the court, fabricate evidence or breach confidentiality except as the law allows. The Bar Council of India Rules set standards of professional conduct.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Show calm, principle and a practical alternative.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

rounds.q: Your client wants you to file a backdated document. What do you do?
rounds.model: I would refuse, explaining that filing a backdated document misleads the court, may be forgery, and risks the client's case and my licence. I would offer lawful alternatives, such as explaining the real chronology. If the client insists, I would withdraw from the matter.
followups: What if the client says everyone does it?

rounds.q: You discover a senior's citation is wrong the night before arguments. What do you do?
rounds.model: I would verify the citation carefully, then tell the senior privately with the correct authority and a one-line note, so the court is not misled. It protects the client and the senior's credibility.
followups: How would you phrase it politely?

rounds.q: How would you explain a 3-year limitation period to a worried client?
rounds.model: I would say: you generally have three years from the date your right to sue arose, but the exact date depends on the case, so please bring all documents this week so we can calculate it and file in time. I would avoid jargon and confirm the date in writing.
followups: What if the period has just expired?

rounds.q: Describe a time you worked under pressure on a deadline.
rounds.model: In a moot preparation our co-researcher left a week before submission. I divided the remaining issues, set daily checkpoints and proofread citations. We submitted on time and I learned to plan buffers.

rounds.q: Where do you see yourself in five years?
rounds.model: I want to be a confident litigator who drafts well, argues effectively and handles matters independently, while continuing to learn from seniors and serve clients ethically.
followups: Which skill do you most need to build?

uni-llb-core.description: A study companion for LLB students in India: the law of contract, the law of torts, and criminal law under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, BNSS and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (in force from 1 July 2024). courses.title: Law of Contract (Indian Contract Act, 1872)
courses.summary: Offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, free consent, void and voidable agreements, performance, breach and damages, worked through real commercial disputes.
outcomes: Learners can test whether an agreement is a valid contract using section 10
Learners can distinguish void, voidable and unenforceable agreements
Learners can apply coercion, undue influence, fraud and misrepresentation to facts
Learners can explain remedies for breach, including damages

lessons.title: Lab: Is there a valid contract? Section 10 checklist

scenes.text: Arjun messages a seller: I will buy your laptop for 40,000 rupees. The seller replies: Done, collect it tomorrow.
The next day the seller says he got a better offer and refuses. Arjun wonders whether he can sue.

steps.title: Section 10 in one line
steps.body:
All agreements are contracts if made by the **free consent** of parties **competent to contract**, for a **lawful consideration** and with a **lawful object**, and are not expressly declared void. Writing is not always needed; many contracts are valid orally or by messages.

Section 2(h) defines a contract as an agreement enforceable by law.

steps.title: Applying it to Arjun
steps.body:
- Offer: Arjun's message with a price
- Acceptance: the seller's unqualified reply, Done
- Consideration: 40,000 rupees for the laptop
- Capacity: both adults of sound mind
- Object lawful, consent free

So a binding contract likely exists and the seller's refusal is a breach.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a written, stamped document is always necessary
- Confusing an invitation to treat (a shop display, a price list) with an offer
- Forgetting that a social promise like dinner at my house usually lacks intention to create legal relations

activity.prompt: Tick each element you would verify before advising a client that a contract exists
items: It was accepted absolutely and unconditionally
There was consideration from both sides
Parties were competent: adults, sound mind, not disqualified by law
Consent was free of coercion, fraud, mistake and the rest

quiz.why: Section 10 states when agreements become contracts.

lessons.title: Lab: Offer, acceptance and the smoke ball

scenes.text: A company advertises that it will pay 100 pounds to anyone who catches influenza after using its smoke ball as directed, and says it has deposited money in a bank to show sincerity.
Mrs Carlill uses it, catches influenza and claims. The company says an advertisement cannot be an offer.

steps.title: General offers
steps.body:
In Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co (1893) the English court held that an advertisement with a definite promise can be a **general offer** to the whole world, accepted by performing the stated conditions. This reasoning is followed in Indian law.

Acceptance must be absolute, communicated (or by conduct as the offer allows) and match the terms of the offer.

steps.title: Counter-offer and revocation
steps.body:
- A counter-offer (I will pay 38,000) rejects the original offer
- An offer can be revoked before acceptance is complete (section 5)
- Silence cannot be imposed as acceptance by the offeror
- Postal acceptance is complete against the proposer when the letter is posted (section 4)

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Always list the facts in time order: offer, any change, acceptance, then ask whether each step was communicated.

activity.prompt: Put the formation of a contract by post in order
items: A makes a proposal by letter
B receives the letter and decides to accept
A becomes bound; the contract is formed

quiz.q: In Carlill, the advertisement was held to be
quiz.why: The deposit showed serious intention and the promise was definite.
Section 7 requires absolute and unqualified acceptance.

lessons.title: Lab: Free consent and void agreements

scenes.text: Rekha, a widow with little education, signs a loan document at the lender's office after the lender's manager threatens to complain to her employer unless she signs.
Later she asks a lawyer whether the agreement binds her.

steps.title: Consent is free when it is not caused by
steps.body:
- **Coercion** (section 15): committing or threatening an act forbidden by the Indian Penal law, now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, or unlawful detention of property
- **Undue influence** (section 16): a dominant position used to gain unfair advantage
- **Fraud** (section 17): deliberate deceit
- **Misrepresentation** (section 18): innocent false statement
- **Mistake** (sections 20 to 22)

A contract made without free consent is **voidable** at the option of the aggrieved party, except for mutual mistake of fact going to the root, which makes it void.

steps.title: Void and voidable
steps.body:
- **Void**: no legal effect, for example a wagering agreement (section 30), an agreement in restraint of trade (section 27) or with a minor
- **Voidable**: valid until the innocent party rescinds it
- A minor's agreement is void from the start (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose, 1903)

steps.title: Relief
steps.body: The aggrieved party may rescind and may also claim compensation. Delay and affirmation can lose the right to rescind.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – breach and damages

scenes.text: A bakery orders an oven from a supplier for delivery on 1 March. The supplier delivers it on 30 March and the bakery loses a large festival order.
The bakery claims lost profits; the supplier says it did not know about the festival order.

steps.title: Remedies
steps.body:
Under section 73, the party who suffers breach is entitled to compensation for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things or that the parties knew, when they made the contract, would be likely to result. **Remote** or indirect loss is not recoverable. This follows Hadley v Baxendale.

Section 74 allows reasonable compensation up to the stipulated sum where a contract names a penalty or liquidated damages. The injured party must still prove loss in many cases. Specific performance and injunction come under the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

steps.title: Mitigation
steps.body: The innocent party must take reasonable steps to reduce loss, for example by hiring a replacement oven. Loss that could have been avoided is not recoverable.

steps.title: Frustration
steps.body: Section 56: a contract to do an act that becomes impossible or unlawful afterwards becomes void when the act becomes impossible.

steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

lessons.title: Lab: Negligence – the snail in the bottle

story.title: A cafe, a bottle and a bad surprise

scenes.text: In 1928 a woman drank ginger beer from an opaque bottle bought by a friend and later found a decomposed snail, becoming ill.
She had no contract with the shopkeeper. Could she sue the manufacturer?

steps.title: The elements
steps.body: Negligence needs: (1) a **duty of care** owed to the claimant, (2) **breach** of that duty by falling below the standard of a reasonable person, and (3) **damage** caused by the breach, not too remote. Donoghue v Stevenson (1932) created the neighbour principle: take reasonable care to avoid acts you can reasonably foresee would injure your neighbour.

steps.title: Indian practice
steps.body: Courts apply the same elements. Medical negligence, road accidents and defective products are common cases; consumers may also use the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

steps.title: Res ipsa loquitur
steps.body: Where the thing speaks for itself, for example a surgical instrument left inside a patient, the burden shifts to the defendant to explain.

lessons.title: Lab: Strict and absolute liability

scenes.text: A chemical plant in a crowded city leaks oleum gas. Many nearby residents are injured.

steps.title: From Rylands to M.C. Mehta
steps.body:
Rylands v Fletcher (1868): a person who brings onto land something likely to do mischief if it escapes is liable for the damage, subject to exceptions such as act of God or the claimant's consent.

In M.C. Mehta v Union of India (1987), the Supreme Court of India evolved **absolute liability**: an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity is liable for harm, with **no exceptions**, and the compensation should relate to the size and capacity of the enterprise.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not say the Indian rule is the same as Rylands. India removed the exceptions for hazardous industries.

scenes.text: A diner posts a false claim that a restaurant uses expired meat. Next door, a resident burns waste daily and smoke enters a neighbour's flat.

steps.title: Two torts
steps.body:
**Defamation**: a false statement that lowers a person's reputation in the eyes of right-thinking people, published to a third party. Libel is in permanent form; slander is spoken. Defences include truth (justification), fair comment on a matter of public interest and privilege.

**Nuisance**: unlawful interference with use or enjoyment of land. Private nuisance affects individuals; public nuisance affects the community. Remedies: damages and injunction.

steps.title: Care
steps.body: Criminal defamation also exists in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Vicarious liability
steps.body: An employer is liable for torts committed by an employee **in the course of employment**. The test asks whether the act was authorised or an unauthorised mode of doing an authorised act. An independent contractor's torts generally do not make the principal liable, with exceptions. Remedies include compensation and, for road accidents, claims before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal.

lessons.title: Lab: Three new laws – which one answers which question?

scenes.text: Nisha finds old notes quoting IPC and CrPC. Her professor says those codes were replaced from 1 July 2024.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: The three replacements
steps.body:
- **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023** replaced the Indian Penal Code (substantive offences and punishments)
- **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023** replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure
- **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023** replaced the Indian Evidence Act

They apply to offences committed on or after 1 July 2024; older offences are dealt with under the earlier laws.

steps.title: Old cases
steps.body: Judgments citing IPC sections remain important for principles. Always map the old section to the new one using the official correspondence tables.

steps.title: Do not say
steps.body: Do not present IPC or CrPC as the current law for new offences.

lessons.title: Lab: Actus reus, mens rea and stages of a crime

scenes.text: Dev buys a knife intending to harm a rival, waits outside his house, then walks away without acting.
At what stage did Dev cross into criminal liability, if at all?

steps.title: General principles
steps.body:
A crime usually needs a guilty act (**actus reus**) and a guilty mind (**mens rea**). The stages are: intention, preparation, attempt, commission. Intention and mere preparation are generally not punishable, but an attempt, which comes close to the completed act, usually is. Some serious preparations (for example to wage war or make counterfeit tools) are separately offences.

Chapter III of the BNS lists general exceptions such as acts of a child below the age fixed by law, unsoundness of mind, accident, necessity and private defence.

steps.title: Murder and culpable homicide
steps.body: BNS section 103 prescribes punishment for murder and section 105 for culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Both turn on intention and knowledge; the difference is the degree of likelihood of death and the circumstances.

steps.title: Sections
steps.body: Check the Act text and an official correspondence table for exact section numbers before citing.

steps.title: Process under the BNSS
steps.body:
- **Information** about a cognizable offence is recorded as an FIR (section 173). A **zero FIR** can be registered at any police station and transferred. Information may also be given electronically and then signed within the prescribed time.
- **Investigation**: statements, evidence collection, forensic examination for serious offences, arrest following the rules, and a police report on completion.
- **Bail and remand**: bailable offences give bail as of right; for others a court decides. Production before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest.
- **Trial**: cognizance, charges, evidence, arguments, judgment, and appeal.

steps.title: Theft and cheating
steps.body: Theft is defined in BNS section 303 and cheating in section 318, with snatching as a separate offence.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – is the electronic record admissible?

scenes.text: A complainant produces a printout of chat messages as proof of a threat. The defence says it is easily edited.
The judge asks whether the required certificate was filed.

steps.title: Evidence under the BSA
steps.body:
The BSA treats **electronic records** as documents. Section 63 requires a certificate, in the prescribed form, from the person in charge of the device and an expert, so that the court can trust the record's origin and integrity. Primary evidence is the original; secondary evidence is allowed only in defined cases.

A confession made to a police officer is generally not admissible against the accused, subject to the discovery rule. The burden of proof in criminal cases is on the prosecution, beyond reasonable doubt.
